q: When conversation history exceeds useful model context, who should determine what remains available to the model?
a: Make memory explicit as user-manipulable objects rather than leaving management entirely behind the interface.

q: What unit should users manipulate when controlling an agent’s memory?
a: A “memory object”: an interactive piece of conversational history that can be moved, edited, deleted, or summarized with others.

q: Should the user-facing memory representation match the context actually exposed to the model?
a: Yes: the front-end representation is what the LLM “sees” on the back end—a shared representation/common ground.

q: When a user’s intent or conversational context changes, what should determine whether an existing memory can influence the next response?
a: The user toggles each object visible or hidden; hidden objects are grayed out.

q: When context is missing, who may add memory and in what form?
a: The user may add a new memory object to supplement context.

q: When a stored representation is inaccurate or stale, should correction modify the existing memory, append a correction, or preserve versions?
a: The user directly edits the existing object to refine or update context.

q: When memory is irrelevant or unwanted, should removal erase it, hide it temporarily, or retain a suppression record?
a: Delete completely irrelevant context; hiding is separately available for temporary exclusion.

q: When multiple memories compete for limited/context-sensitive model attention, should ordering be system-selected or user-controlled?
a: All objects are draggable; users can refine ordering and placement because context position affects model use.

q: When memory must be compressed, who chooses the inputs to compression?
a: The user selects the memory objects to be summarized by the LLM.

q: After compression, should the summary replace, coexist with, or point back to its source material?
a: The LLM creates a new summary memory object; the original conversation remains viewable by clicking the summary; the summary can be refined.

q: When context should cross conversation boundaries, should it be copied, referenced, re-derived, or globally retrieved?
a: Users drag a memory into another conversation; it is copied by reference so its source remains identifiable.

q: When the same memory is shared among conversations, what should happen when it is edited at the source or destination?
a: Underspecified. “Copied by reference” is stated, but synchronization, mutability, permissions, and deletion propagation are not.

q: Should memories represent what was said, what the system inferred, or both—and how should their epistemic status be exposed?
a: The paper primarily treats memory as conversational history or its summary; no epistemic tiers are specified.

q: When content concerns someone other than the user, what should be eligible for durable retention?
a: Underspecified. The paper exposes and shares conversational history without a discussed third-party retention boundary.

q: Which categories of otherwise inferable information should be structurally excluded from memory?
a: Underspecified. No sensitive-category exclusion, psychological-inference boundary, or logged rejection mechanism is described.

q: What should trigger creation of a durable memory from incoming conversation?
a: Underspecified. Objects are described as conversational history and can be added or summarized, but automatic segmentation/extraction criteria and timing are absent.

q: When a new statement conflicts with existing memory, what should determine which belief is active?
a: Underspecified. User editing/deleting can repair context, but contradiction detection and resolution are not described.

q: When answering a new request, how should candidate memories be retrieved and ranked?
a: User-visible objects constitute context, and visibility/order control access and placement; any automatic retrieval, ranking, context budget, or tie-breaking is underspecified.

q: Should the system expose memories that were retrieved but not used or not permitted in the answer?
a: The interface shows objects visible to the LLM, but it does not distinguish retrieved, attended-to, used-in-output, or withheld-by-policy states.

q: When the system lacks adequate memory, should it guess, ask, abstain, or expose near matches?
a: Underspecified. Conversational breakdown repair motivates control, but no runtime uncertainty/abstention behavior is specified.

q: When users correct or confirm memories, when should the system interrupt them?
a: User manipulation is available directly; prompting policy and attention budget are underspecified.

q: As time passes without confirming evidence, should a memory remain stable, decay, expire, or be revalidated?
a: Underspecified. No time model, decay, expiration, or revalidation is described.

q: Which product surfaces should have access to which classes of memory?
a: Multiple conversations/agents can receive shared objects; no task- or surface-specific retrieval rights are described.

q: How much memory-management complexity should be continuously visible to the user?
a: A 2D canvas exposes objects and supports toggling, dragging, editing, deleting, combining, creating conversations, and sharing.

q: What happens when the memory system itself is wrong about what it stored, summarized, or exposed?
a: Users can edit/delete memory and inspect original conversation behind a summary; no automatic detection, rollback semantics, or harm-specific recovery is specified.
